turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, thank you for seeing me. I guess, well, the main reason I'm here, what finally pushed me to actually make an appointment and come in today, is this ongoing issue I've been having with my work. I just finished my bachelor's degree—art history, actually, which I really loved, but now I'm in that weird phase of having no job and just applying for absolutely everything. Internships, entry-level stuff, you name it. And I've been doing some research on the side for one of my old professors just to stay busy and build my resume. 

But the thing is, I keep turning in these applications, or handing over my research notes, with these really small but just incredibly embarrassing mistakes. Like, last week, I submitted this whole write-up and I completely mislabeled an artwork date. I was off by a whole century on a piece I know perfectly well! Or I'll be filling out an important application and just completely skip a question, like my eyes just glide right over it and my brain doesn't even register that it's there. 

And the most frustrating part—the part that really makes me feel like I'm losing my mind—is that I honestly thought I had checked them. I sit there, I proofread the document, I go over it, I tell myself, "Okay, this is perfect, it's ready to send," and then boom, the professor points out a glaring error, or I get an email back saying my form is incomplete. It's happening so much that I'm terrified I'm ruining my chances before my career even starts, and I just don't understand how I can look right at a mistake and not see it until it's too late.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly describes making careless mistakes, such as mislabeling dates and skipping questions on applications, despite attempting to proofread their work.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been experiencing these kinds of mistakes and attention problems? Did this start recently after you graduated, or have you noticed similar issues with focus and catching errors going back further—like during college or even earlier?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's definitely not a brand new thing, but it really, really became obvious after I graduated. I mean, I moved to Boston right after I finished my bachelor's—which was a huge transition, you know? Finding an apartment, figuring out the T, just adjusting to being out of the college bubble and trying to set up a real adult life. And it was around that time, when I was trying to get all my ducks in a row and start applying for things in a new city, that I really started noticing how bad it was getting. 

So, I guess, if I trace it back to when I got to Boston and really started grinding on these applications and doing this research for my professor... it's been about a year and eleven months. Yeah, almost two full years of just... constantly missing things. I mean, in college, I guess there were times I’d lose points on a paper for a dumb typo, but it felt different then. You know, you’re pulling an all-nighter, you’re drinking too much coffee, everyone makes mistakes when they’re sleep-deprived. But here in Boston, I’m getting enough sleep, I’m sitting at my desk in my apartment, I’m looking right at the screen in broad daylight, and I’m still just... completely missing a whole question on a fellowship application or spelling a curator's name wrong after staring at it for five minutes. It’s like, ever since I made that move and the stakes got higher, this whole issue just became impossible to ignore. So yeah, about a year and eleven months of really dealing with this specific level of frustration.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes constantly missing things, such as skipping a whole question on an application or misspelling a name despite staring at it.
symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient explicitly states that they are getting enough sleep, denying sleep deprivation or disturbance as the cause of their current issues.

turns.doctor_question: Besides work and applications, do you find yourself having trouble focusing or missing details in other areas of your life—like when you're reading for pleasure, managing your personal finances, or doing everyday tasks at home?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, definitely. It's... it's really not just the work stuff, which is part of why it's so frustrating. It bleeds into pretty much everything else, especially all those normal, everyday adult things I’m supposed to be on top of now. 

Like, for instance, just the other day, I got an email from my landlord about renewing the lease, or well, a question about a maintenance thing, and I read it on my phone while I was making breakfast. I told myself, "Okay, I need to reply to this as soon as I finish my eggs." I even mentally drafted the response! I knew exactly what I was going to say. But then I put my plate in the sink, maybe got distracted by a podcast or something, and... it was just gone. Completely dropped out of my mind. It wasn't until like four days later when I got a follow-up email from him that I even remembered it existed. I felt so stupid. 

And it happens with bills, too, which is honestly kind of scary because I don't have a lot of money right now. I’ll get a notification for my internet bill, and I’ll think, "Right, pay that today," and then I just... don't. It just evaporates from my brain. Or groceries! I'll walk to Trader Joe's—which is a whole ordeal anyway because it's always so crowded and overwhelming—and I'll have this very specific list in my head of what I need for the week. I'll need, like, milk, eggs, and spinach. And I'll walk out with coffee, some weird seasonal snack, and totally forget the milk. It’s like my brain just can’t hold onto these basic tasks. I mean to do them, I really do, but then days go by and I realize I never actually followed through. It's exhausting constantly feeling like I'm dropping the ball on just... existing.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes getting distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as a podcast, which causes them to lose track of tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly describes frequently forgetting daily activities and errands, such as replying to emails, paying bills, and buying intended groceries.

turns.doctor_question: When you were in elementary school or middle school, did teachers or parents ever mention that you had trouble paying attention, or did you struggle to keep track of assignments and homework back then?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yeah, actually. It's funny you ask that, because for a long time I sort of convinced myself that this was all just a recent problem, you know? Just adulting being hard. But if I really think back to being a kid, like elementary and middle school... yeah, the signs were definitely there. It just looked a little different because, well, I was a kid and I had my parents basically running my life. 

I remember, vividly, my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was this very strict, very organized woman who loved color-coding everything—and she would always, always write these notes on my report cards. It was always the same tune. She’d say things like, "He has such wonderful, creative ideas during class discussions," or "He really understands the material," but then there was always a "but." It was always, "But he forgets to turn in his worksheets," or "He loses the instruction packets," or "He rushes and misses the little details on his math tests." 

And it wasn't just her. It was a recurring theme. I mean, my backpack was like a black hole. I would do the homework—I swear I would do it, sitting at the kitchen table while my mom cooked dinner—and then I would shove it in a folder, put the folder in my bag, and by the time I got to school the next morning, it was just... gone. Or I'd forget to even take the assignment out of my bag to hand it in. My parents actually had to institute this whole routine where every single night, without fail, my dad would sit down with me, dump my entire backpack out on the living room rug, and we would go through every single piece of paper. He had to check my planner, check my folders, make sure the pencils were actually in the pencil case and not just floating around at the bottom getting graphite on everything. 

If they hadn't done that, if my parents hadn't been acting as my external brain, checking my backpack every single night, I probably would have failed half my classes just from missing little details or losing things. So, yeah... I guess when I really look at it, I've always struggled with this stuff. It’s just that back then, I had this whole support system making sure I didn't completely fall apart, and now it's just me trying to keep track of it all, and clearly, I'm not doing a great job of it.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient recalls teachers noting that he rushed and missed little details on his math tests.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes his backpack as a 'black hole' and needing his parents to organize his folders and supplies every night.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly mentions losing instruction packets, losing completed homework, and generally struggling with losing things.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever gone through periods where you felt like you had a lot more energy than usual, or where you needed much less sleep than normal but still felt really energized and productive—maybe lasting for several days or a week or so?
turns.patient_response:
No, honestly... I mean, I kind of wish I had that problem, to be honest with you. If anything, I am the exact opposite. I love sleep. I really, really need my sleep. Like, if I don't get my solid seven or eight hours, I am just a complete zombie the next day. 

I know some people get like that, you know? Like, I had this roommate sophomore year who would just go on these absolute tears where he'd be up for three days straight working on a coding project and he’d seem totally fine, just buzzing around the kitchen making pasta at 3 AM. But me? No way. I mean, sure, if I'm super stressed about a deadline—like those fellowship applications I was talking about earlier—I might force myself to stay up late, drinking way too much iced coffee just to keep my eyes open. But I never actually feel *energized* when I do that. I feel exactly as exhausted and miserable as a person should feel when they're sleep-deprived. My brain just gets even foggier, which is really saying something given how much I already struggle with missing details on a normal day! 

So, yeah, I never have those periods where I just wake up super early, ready to conquer the world and, I don't know, deep-clean my entire apartment or write a novel on three hours of sleep. I'm usually dragging myself out of bed, hitting snooze at least three or four times, just trying to muster up the willpower to make my eggs and face the day. Even when I have a relatively productive afternoon, it's not because I have some crazy battery pack of energy, it's just that I finally managed to sit still for an hour. So, no, definitely no sudden surges of superhuman energy or going days without sleep. I can't even fathom what that would actually feel like.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly states they 'struggle with missing details on a normal day'.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly denies having 'sudden surges of superhuman energy' or feeling energized.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient denies needing less sleep, stating they 'really, really need my sleep' and would be a 'zombie' without 7-8 hours.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself fidgeting a lot, or do you have trouble sitting still? Like, when you're trying to focus on work or reading, do you feel restless or have an urge to move around, tap your leg, or do something with your hands?
turns.patient_response:
Not really, no. I mean... my brain is definitely bouncing all over the place, kind of like a pinball machine, but my body? My body is actually pretty still. When I sit down at my desk in my room to try and get through those fellowship applications I mentioned, or even just when I'm trying to read a book on the couch, I don't really feel that... that physical urge to get up and pace around. 

I know exactly what you mean, though, because I've seen people do it. Like, back when I was in college, studying in the library, you'd always see guys just violently shaking their legs under the table, or they'd be constantly clicking a pen—click, click, click—which, honestly, used to distract me so much when I was already struggling to just get through a single paragraph of my reading. But I never really did that myself.

For me, it's more like... I just sit there. Sometimes I'll sit in the exact same position for, like, an hour or two, just staring completely blankly at my laptop screen. I'll be totally zoned out, maybe thinking about a movie I watched three years ago or wondering if I should buy a different brand of coffee, but I'm not physically restless at all. I don't have this pent-up physical energy that I need to burn off. If anything, I get kind of locked into place physically while my thoughts just completely drift away into the ether. So, yeah, I don't really tap my fingers or feel the need to mess with a stress ball or constantly shift in my seat or anything like that. It's really just the mental focus that totally falls apart, rather than an inability to physically sit in a chair.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (others clicking pens) and unrelated thoughts (drifting off to think about an old movie).
symptom_reasoning.S059: The patient reports struggling to read a single paragraph, staring blankly at the screen, and experiencing their mental focus totally falling apart.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies tapping their fingers, messing with objects, or shifting in their seat.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient denies the urge to get up and pace, noting they often sit in the exact same position for hours.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly states they are 'not physically restless at all' and do not have pent-up physical energy.

turns.doctor_question: Do people ever tell you that you talk a lot or interrupt them frequently? Or have you noticed that you tend to dominate conversations or have trouble waiting your turn to speak?
turns.patient_response:
You know, it’s interesting you phrase it like that. I wouldn't say I'm someone who just constantly interrupts people in normal, everyday chit-chat, like if we're just talking about the weather or what we had for lunch or something. But... well, especially back in college—which, you know, wasn't that long ago for me since I just finished my bachelor's—when we were in these upper-level seminars, it definitely happened. 

My major involved a lot of really small, discussion-based classes, so a lot of our grade was based on participation and breaking down these really complex theoretical texts. And sometimes, we'd be sitting around the seminar table, or even out doing a site visit, having these really deep gallery conversations while standing in front of a piece... and someone would bring up a point, and I would just get *so* excited. Like, genuinely thrilled about the idea. 

I'd start explaining my thought process, trying to connect it to, I don't know, a different movement or a specific essay we read two weeks prior, and I just... I get totally swept up in it. I'll explain an idea for way, way too long, going down all these little conceptual rabbit holes to make sure my point is perfectly articulated and that everyone follows my exact train of logic. And I'm usually just looking at the artwork, or looking at my hands while I talk, and then... I don't know, it’s like I suddenly wake up from a trance. I'll finally finish my thought and look around the circle, and I'll realize afterward that I just completely monopolized the entire discussion. 

Like, I'll realize that I barely left any space for anyone else to respond or even get a word in edgewise. It's not that I *want* to dominate the conversation or that I think I'm the smartest guy in the room, it's really just that the enthusiasm kind of hijacks my brain. I just get so hyper-focused on getting the idea out of my head and into the open that I completely forget about the basic social rhythm of a conversation. I always feel a little guilty about it when I walk out of the building, replaying it in my head and thinking, "Man, you really didn't let Sarah finish her point at all, did you?" So, yeah, in those specific academic or intellectual settings, I definitely have a habit of talking way too much.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient admits to explaining ideas for 'way, way too long' and completely monopolizing discussions, leaving no space for others to speak.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient acknowledges interrupting others, noting they realize afterward that they 'didn't let Sarah finish her point at all'.

turns.doctor_question: When you're working on something you're really passionate about—like your art history research or looking at artwork—do you ever get so absorbed in it that hours just fly by and you lose track of time completely?
turns.patient_response:
You would think so, right? I mean, because I really do love art history. I spent four years studying it, and obviously, I'm trying to get these fellowships now, so it’s something I care deeply about. But honestly... no, not really. I don't think I ever get that thing where I just completely lose track of time. 

If anything, it's the exact opposite, which is actually incredibly frustrating for me. Like, I'll go to a museum—say I'm going to look at a Caravaggio, which I absolutely love, you know, the chiaroscuro is just incredible, the drama in the composition is so intense. I'll stand in front of it, and for the first maybe five or ten minutes, I am really, truly engaged. I'm looking at the brushstrokes, I'm analyzing the way the light hits the figures, I'm thinking about the historical context. But then... I don't know, my brain just can't seem to hold onto that level of engagement for very long. 

Instead of getting sucked in for hours, I'll suddenly start wondering how long the security guard has been standing in that one spot, or I'll notice a tiny smudge on the wall next to the placard, or I'll just randomly remember that I forgot to buy paper towels at the grocery store. And it’s the same thing with my research. When I was writing my senior thesis on post-war abstract expressionism—which was a topic I picked myself, something I was genuinely so passionate about—it was still a total slog. I’d sit down at the library with this huge stack of really fascinating books, feeling super motivated, but I’d read one page, maybe two, and then I’m checking my phone. Or I’m staring out the window at people walking across the quad. Or I'm just looking at the clock.

I am *always* looking at the clock. I never have that experience where people say, "Oh wow, I looked up and it was suddenly dark outside!" For me, I'm acutely aware of every single minute passing because it feels like a constant, active struggle to keep my attention on the text or the artwork. I'll be thinking, "Okay, it's been twenty minutes, maybe I can justify taking a quick break to get a coffee." So, yeah, even when it's my absolute favorite subject in the world, I don't get lost in it. I really wish I did, because it would make getting through this fellowship research so much easier, but my brain just always wants to pull away and look at something else.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a constant, active struggle to keep their attention on texts or artwork for very long, even when highly motivated.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient reports being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli like a smudge on the wall or unrelated thoughts about buying groceries.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient explicitly states they still deeply care about and love art history, indicating no loss of interest in their passions.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned you struggle to stay focused even on things you love, like art history. But I'm curious—have there ever been times, maybe with a hobby or something outside of work or school, where you got so completely absorbed that you genuinely did lose track of time? Like, you started doing something and suddenly realized hours had passed?
turns.patient_response:
I have actually thought about that a lot because I see other people do it all the time. Like my old roommate from sophomore year, he could sit down and play a video game for literally nine hours straight. He would completely forget to eat, forget to drink water, just totally locked into the screen. But for me, I mean... no. Not even with hobbies. It is honestly the exact same feeling as the art history stuff. 

Take the guitar, for example. My parents got me this really nice acoustic guitar for graduation a few months ago, and I was so excited about it. I have always wanted to be one of those guys who can just pick up an instrument and play, and I really genuinely want to learn. So I will sit on the edge of my bed, I will pull up a tutorial on my laptop, and I will start practicing a chord progression. But even then, doing something purely for fun, with zero pressure, I just cannot stay in the zone. 

I will practice for maybe ten or fifteen minutes, and then I am immediately looking at the time on my phone. Or I will start wondering if the strings need to be replaced already, or I will hear a car drive by outside and start wondering where they are going in such a hurry. It is like my internal clock is just way too loud. It is always ticking in the background, making me hyper-aware of every minute that passes. I never get that feeling where the rest of the world just melts away. I will be playing a video game or watching a movie I was really looking forward to, and after twenty minutes I am pausing it to check my email or just staring at the wall. So yeah, I really do not think I have ever had that experience of looking up and realizing hours have flown by, not with anything. I am always just painfully aware of the time.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention even during leisure activities like playing guitar, video games, or watching movies, typically losing focus after 10 to 20 minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as hearing a car drive by, and having unrelated thoughts while trying to focus on a hobby.

turns.doctor_question: I hear you about the constant time awareness. But let me ask this differently—has there ever been a time, maybe just once or twice, where you got so caught up in something—anything at all—that you genuinely forgot to eat, or someone had to tell you to stop because hours had actually passed without you noticing?
turns.patient_response:
I get why you're asking, and I know I'm probably sounding like a broken record here, but... really, genuinely, no. Not even once. I mean, the eating thing especially—I never, ever forget to eat. My stomach is honestly like a secondary clock. If it hits 12:30 or 1:00, I am acutely aware that it is lunchtime, regardless of what I'm doing. 

Even if I was in the middle of, say, formatting the bibliography for my senior thesis—which, let me tell you, is an absolute nightmare process where you'd think someone might just put their head down and power through it just to get it over with—I just couldn't do it. I'd be staring at the Chicago Manual of Style, trying to figure out where the commas are supposed to go for a translated text that has both an editor and a primary author, which is incredibly tedious, and I'd still be thinking, "Okay, it's 12:35, I should probably go make a turkey sandwich." I just... I don't have that gear in my brain. I really don't. 

I've actually tried to force it, too, just to see if I could make it happen. Like, I'll put my phone in another room, close all the extra tabs on my browser, and just try to lock myself into a task, thinking maybe *this* is the time I'll finally get that tunnel vision everyone talks about. But instead of getting caught up in the work, I just end up feeling this weird, restless pressure, like I'm trapped in the room with the task. I'll start wondering what time it is, and since my phone is in the other room, that actually makes it worse. Then I'm just obsessing over how long it's been since I put the phone away. Has it been an hour? Has it been ten minutes? Is it raining outside now? And eventually, I just have to get up and go check. 

So, no, nobody has ever had to tap me on the shoulder and pull me out of a trance, and I've definitely never skipped a meal by accident. I'm just always, always present in the time that's passing, minute by minute, even when I desperately wish I wasn't.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention on tasks, noting that even when trying to force focus, they cannot stay locked into the work.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient experiences unrelated thoughts while trying to work, such as wondering what time it is or if it is raining outside.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient notes that when trying to stay seated and focused on a task, they eventually 'just have to get up and go check' on things like their phone or the time.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes experiencing a 'weird, restless pressure' when trying to force themselves to sit and focus on a task.

turns.doctor_question: I know you've said you don't lose track of time, but I want to ask about something slightly different. Have you ever had a moment—even just for a few minutes—where you felt completely locked in or in a zone, where your attention felt *sharp* and *narrow* rather than scattered? Like, where you were so zeroed in on one specific thing that distractions just didn't bother you at all?
turns.patient_response:
I mean... no, not really. I'm trying to think of a time where my focus felt like a laser beam like you're describing, where everything else just sort of fell away and I was completely zeroed in, but honestly, my brain just doesn't seem to work that way. It's never sharp or narrow. It's always sort of... wide open, taking in everything all at once, which is why it feels so scattered. 

Like, even if I'm doing something that requires a lot of precision, my mind is still bouncing around. For instance, when I was putting together this IKEA bookshelf for my new apartment—which, by the way, was a complete disaster because the instructions are just pictures and I kept losing the little wooden dowels—you would think that would be a moment where I'd have to be hyper-focused, right? Because if you mess up one step, you have to take the whole thing apart. But even then, I wasn't locked in. I was trying to screw in a bolt, but at the same time, I was listening to a podcast about the history of the Medici family, and I was wondering if I should order Thai food for dinner, and I was noticing that the paint on the baseboard was starting to chip. 

There's never a point where the background noise turns off. The distractions are always there, and they always bother me. I never get that feeling of being in the zone, even for a few minutes. It's more like I'm constantly juggling five different thoughts, and I'm just trying to keep the one that's most important—like writing a paper or reading a book—from dropping. But the other thoughts never go away. They're always right there, pulling at my attention. So, yeah, I don't think I've ever experienced that sharp, narrow focus you're talking about. It's always just a million things at once.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes their focus as never sharp or narrow, always scattered, and constantly struggling to keep their attention on the most important task without dropping it.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly mentions losing the small wooden dowels necessary for assembling their bookshelf.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being constantly pulled away by extraneous stimuli (chipping paint) and unrelated thoughts (ordering Thai food) while trying to complete a task.

turns.doctor_question: I want to go back to something for a moment. You mentioned your art history seminars in college, where you'd get excited about ideas and end up talking for a long time. In those moments when you were really passionate and explaining your thoughts to the group, did it ever feel like your focus was actually really sharp and locked onto what you were saying—like you were completely absorbed in getting that idea across, even if you were talking too much?
turns.patient_response:
Well, see, that's an interesting way to put it, because... I guess it feels different from focus, if that makes sense? It's not like I'm locked in on the *task* of explaining, it's more like... like a dam breaking. Like I have all these thoughts about, say, the use of light in Caravaggio's later works, and how it reflects this sort of existential dread, and suddenly I just have to get it all out. 

But even then, I wouldn't call it sharp or narrow focus, because my brain is still going a million miles an hour. I'm connecting this painting to that historical event, and then thinking about a critique I read, and then remembering a conversation I had with my professor... and I'm just talking and talking. And it's true, in those seminars or even if I'm just at a gallery with friends and we're looking at something I really care about, I get so wound up and excited. The ideas are just spilling out, and I'm trying to explain all the nuances and the context and why it's so important... 

But the thing is, I'm not really *focused* on the conversation as a two-way street. It's more like I'm just releasing all this built-up energy. And then, you know, I'll finally take a breath, and I'll look around, and I'll realize... oh, wow, I've been talking for like, ten solid minutes. And I'll see the other students sort of politely waiting, or maybe my friend is looking a little glazed over, and I realize I barely left any space for anyone else to respond or get a word in edgewise. I just sort of bulldoze the conversation because I'm so eager to explain the idea, but it doesn't feel like being "in the zone"—it feels more like I just lost my brakes for a minute. So, yeah, I do talk way too much when I get going on those topics, but it's not that sharp, laser focus you're talking about. It's just... a lot of words coming out very fast.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient confirms talking for ten solid minutes and bulldozing conversations without leaving space for others to respond.
symptom_reasoning.S037: The patient describes their speech as a 'dam breaking' where they 'have to get it all out,' with words coming out very fast and feeling like they 'lost their brakes.'
symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient explicitly states their brain is 'going a million miles an hour' as they rapidly connect different ideas and thoughts.

turns.doctor_question: When you're in one of those art history discussions and you're really excited, explaining your ideas—in that moment, do you find it hard to *stop* talking, or do you feel like you could just keep going and going with that topic if nobody interrupted you?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, one hundred percent. If nobody interrupted me, I could probably keep going until the gallery closed or the class ended. It is incredibly hard to stop once I get that momentum going. 

It’s like... you know when you pull a loose thread on a sweater and it just keeps unraveling, and the more you pull, the more string comes out? That’s exactly what it feels like when I’m explaining these ideas. Because in art history, everything is so interconnected, right? You can’t just talk about, say, the use of a specific blue pigment in a Renaissance painting without talking about the trade routes to Afghanistan where the lapis lazuli came from, and you can't talk about that without talking about the economic status of the patron who commissioned the piece... so my brain just keeps feeding me the next logical connection, and the next one, and the next one. 

So if I'm in a seminar, or if I'm walking through a gallery with friends, I just get so excited about an idea and I end up explaining it for way, way too long. I just want them to see all the fascinating layers that I'm seeing! But the problem is, I get so caught up in making sure I'm giving them all the proper context that I completely lose track of the actual social dynamic of the conversation. I just keep going and going. 

And I honestly don't even notice I'm doing it until I finally hit a wall or run out of breath. It’s only afterward, when the silence kind of settles in, that I realize I barely left any space for anyone else to respond. Like, at all. I'll just look at my friend or my classmates and think, "Wow, I just talked *at* you for a solid ten minutes and didn't even ask what you thought of the painting." It’s a terrible feeling, honestly, because I don't mean to dominate the room, but in the moment, the brakes just completely disappear and I just can't seem to stop myself from getting every single thought out of my head.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient explicitly states they talk for 'way, way too long,' keep going without leaving space for others to respond, and find it incredibly hard to stop talking once they start.

turns.doctor_question: When you're in those art history discussions and you're talking about something you're passionate about, and you finally do stop—either because someone interrupts you or class ends—do you feel satisfied, like you got everything out that you needed to say? Or do you feel like you could have kept going indefinitely, like there's always more to explain?
turns.patient_response:
Satisfied? Um, no, definitely not satisfied. I mean, like I was just saying, I could absolutely keep going indefinitely. There is always, always more to explain. It is never a feeling of okay, I have perfectly summarized the entire socio-political climate of seventeenth-century Rome, my work here is done. Because you just can't ever perfectly summarize it! So when class ends, or when we have to move on to the next exhibit in the gallery, or if someone finally jumps in to cut me off, I actually feel a little bit unsettled at first. Like there are all these loose ends I still need to tie up for them and I didn't get the chance to finish painting the whole picture. 

But then, almost immediately after that feeling, the guilt completely takes over. Because, like I mentioned a second ago, that is the exact moment the spell breaks and I realize what I have actually been doing. I will be in a seminar, just completely fired up and excited, explaining an idea for way, way too long, and then the professor will gently suggest we hear from another student, and the reality of the situation just hits me. I look around the table and realize I barely left a single millimeter of space for anyone else to respond or share their own thoughts. It is honestly so embarrassing. I get so wrapped up in the thrill of the idea that I completely forget a conversation is supposed to involve other people participating. 

And the crazy part is, even with that embarrassment washing over me, my brain is still quietly finishing the rest of the thought in my head. I am sitting there feeling terrible about dominating the discussion, but internally I am still thinking about all the historical footnotes and architectural details I didn't get to mention. So yeah, I never really feel like I got everything out. I just eventually run out of time or someone stops me, and then I have to sit there with the realization that I just talked everyone's ear off again without letting them get a word in.
